value.body: Builds the computer systems hidden inside products — cars, appliances, medical devices, meters and industrial controllers — combining microcontroller hardware with the software that runs on it. Employers include automotive suppliers, consumer-electronics and industrial-automation firms, and engineering-services companies. A day mixes writing C code, testing it on a development board and debugging with lab instruments.

items.label: Typical entry
items.value: B.Tech / B.E. in ECE or EEE
items.note: Also EIE and CSE graduates with hardware interest

items.label: Common tools
items.value: C/C++, microcontroller IDEs, debuggers, oscilloscope, logic analyser

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Freshers usually enter through campus hiring at engineering-services or automotive firms, or as trainees at smaller product companies. Hands-on microcontroller projects, a working knowledge of C and the basics of communication protocols (UART, SPI, I2C) carry weight in interviews. Some take a post-graduate diploma in embedded systems design (offered by C-DAC and others) before applying.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Communication protocols — UART, SPI, I2C, CAN
Debugging with oscilloscopes and on-chip debuggers

value.title: At a glance
items: Overlaps heavily with firmware engineering; the two titles are often used interchangeably.
Growth paths: senior engineer → technical lead or architect, or a move into embedded Linux, automotive software or IoT.
Much of the work in India is in engineering-services firms designing for overseas clients.
The learning curve is steep at first; hardware–software bugs take patience to track down.
